One of the sons of king Jehoshaphat ([2 Chr. 21:2](#2Chr.21.2), [4](#2Chr.21.4)). He was murdered by his brother Jehoram.
The first in rank of the priests of the family of Kohathites ([1 Chr. 23:20](#1Chr.23.20)).

The son of Gemariah. He reported to the king’s officers Jeremiah’s prediction, which he had heard Baruch read ([Jer. 36:11](#Jer.36.11), [13](#Jer.36.13)) from his father Gemariah’s chamber in the temple.
One of those sent out by Jehoshaphat to instruct the people in the law ([2 Chr. 17:7](#2Chr.17.7)).

Rivulet, or who as God?, the younger of Saul’s two daughters by his wife Ahinoam ([1 Sam. 14:49](#1Sam.14.49), [50](#1Sam.14.50)). “Attracted by the graces of his person and the gallantry of his conduct, she fell in love with David and became his wife” (18:20-28). She showed her affection for him by promoting his escape to Naioth when Saul sought his life ([1 Sam. 19:12-17](#1Sam.19.12). Comp. [Ps. 59](#Ps.59). See  TERAPHIM). After this she did not see David for many years. …
Prize of Jehovah, a Benjamite, the father of Uzzi ([1 Chr. 9:8](#1Chr.9.8)).
Strife, the fourth son of Abraham by Keturah, the father of the Midianites ([Gen. 25:2](#Gen.25.2); [1 Chr. 1:32](#1Chr.1.32)).
An officer under Dodai, in the time of David and Solomon ([1 Chr. 27:4](#1Chr.27.4)).
Eloquent, a Levitical musician ([Neh. 12:36](#Neh.12.36)) who took part in the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem.
A chief priest who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel ([Neh. 12:5](#Neh.12.5)), called Mijamin (10:7) and Miniamin (12:17).

The sister of Moses and Aaron ([Ex. 2:4-10](#Exod.2.4); [1 Chr. 6:3](#1Chr.6.3)). Her name is prominent in the history of the Exodus. She is called “the prophetess” ([Ex. 15:20](#Exod.15.20)). She took the lead in the song of triumph after the passage of the Red Sea. She died at Kadesh during the second encampment at that place, toward the close of the wanderings in the wilderness, and was buried there ([Num. 20:1](#Num.20.1)).
[1 Chr. 4:17](#1Chr.4.17), one of the descendants of Judah.
A Levite; the eldest of the three sons of Uzziel ([Ex. 6:22](#Exod.6.22)).
Their cleansing or their beholding, a Benjamite, one of the sons of Elpaal ([1 Chr. 8:12](#1Chr.8.12)).
One of the sons of Ishmael ([Gen. 25:14](#Gen.25.14)), and founder of an Arab tribe.
Fatness, one of the Gadite heroes who gathered to David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:10](#1Chr.12.10)).
Number, one of the Jews who accompanied Zerubbabel from Babylon ([Ezra 2:2](#Ezra.2.2)); called also Mispereth ([Neh. 7:7](#Neh.7.7)).

The dual form of matzor, meaning a “mound” or “fortress,” the name of a people descended from Ham ([Gen. 10:6](#Gen.10.6), [13](#Gen.10.13); [1 Chr. 1:8](#1Chr.1.8), [11](#1Chr.1.11)). It was the name generally given by the Hebrews to the land of Egypt (q.v.), and may denote the two Egypts, the Upper and the Lower. The modern Arabic name for Egypt is Muzr.

Reminding, or remembrancer, a Christian of Jerusalem with whom Paul lodged ([Acts 21:16](#Acts.21.16)). He was apparently a native of Cyprus, like Barnabas (11:19, 20), and was well known to the Christians of Caesarea (4:36). He was an “old disciple” (R.V., “early disciple”), i.e., he had become a Christian in the beginning of the formation of the Church in Jerusalem.

King, the name of the national god of the Ammonites, to whom children were sacrificed by fire. He was the consuming and destroying and also at the same time the purifying fire. In [Amos 5:26](#Amos.5.26), “your Moloch” of the Authorized Version is “your king” in the Revised Version (comp. [Acts 7:43](#Acts.7.43)). Solomon ([1 Kings 11:7](#1Kgs.11.7)) erected a high place for this idol on the Mount of Olives, and from that time till the days of Josiah his worship continued ([2 Kings 23:10](#2Kgs.23.10), [13](#2Kgs.23.13)). In the days of Jehoahaz it was partially restored, but after the Captivity wholly disappeared. …

The son of Jair, of the tribe of Benjamin. It has been alleged that he was carried into captivity with Jeconiah, and hence that he must have been at least one hundred and twenty-nine years old in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus (Xerxes). But the words of Esther do not necessarily lead to this conclusion. It was probably Kish of whom it is said (ver. 6) that he “had been carried away with the captivity.”

Drawn (or Egypt. mesu, “son;” hence Rameses, royal son). On the invitation of Pharaoh ([Gen. 45:17-25](#Gen.45.17)), Jacob and his sons went down into Egypt. This immigration took place probably about 350 years before the birth of Moses. Some centuries before Joseph, Egypt had been conquered by a pastoral Semitic race from Asia, the Hyksos, who brought into cruel subjection the native Egyptians, who were an African race. Jacob and his retinue were accustomed to a shepherd’s life, and on their arrival in Egypt were received with favour by the king, who assigned them the “best of the land”, the land of Goshen, to dwell in. The Hyksos or “shepherd” king who thus showed favour to Joseph and his family was in all probability the Pharaoh Apopi (or Apopis).
The son of Zimri, of the posterity of Saul ([1 Chr. 8:36](#1Chr.8.36), [37](#1Chr.8.37); [9:42](#1Chr.9.42), [43](#1Chr.9.43)).
One of the sons of Caleb ([1 Chr. 2:46](#1Chr.2.46)).
Receding, the second of the two sons of Merari ([Ex. 6:19](#Exod.6.19); [Num. 3:20](#Num.3.20)). His sons were called Mushites ([Num. 3:33](#Num.3.33); [26:58](#Num.26.58)).
Pleasantness, one of the three sons of Caleb, the son of Jephunneh ([1 Chr. 4:15](#1Chr.4.15)).
The daughter of the king of Ammon, one of the wives of Solomon, the only one who appears to have borne him a son, viz., Rehoboam ([1 Kings 14:21](#1Kgs.14.21), [31](#1Kgs.14.31)).
The daughter of Lamech and Zillah ([Gen. 4](#Gen.4): 22).

Pleasantness, a Syrian, the commander of the armies of Benhadad II. in the time of Joram, king of Israel. He was afflicted with leprosy; and when the little Hebrew slave-girl that waited on his wife told her of a prophet in Samaria who could cure her master, he obtained a letter from Benhadad and proceeded with it to Joram. The king of Israel suspected in this some evil design against him, and rent his clothes. Elisha the prophet hearing of this, sent for Naaman, and the strange interview which took place is recorded in [2 Kings 5](#2Kgs.5). The narrative contains all that is known of the Syrian commander. He was cured of his leprosy by dipping himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the word of Elisha. His cure is alluded to by our Lord ([Luke 4:27](#Luke.4.27)).
A girl, the second of Ashur’s two wives, of the tribe of Judah ([1 Chr. 4:5](#1Chr.4.5), [6](#1Chr.4.6)).
Youthful, a military chief in David’s army ([1 Chr. 11:37](#1Chr.11.37)), called also Paarai ([2 Sam. 23:35](#2Sam.23.35)).
Foolish, a descendant of Caleb who dwelt at Maon ([1 Sam. 25](#1Sam.25)), the modern Main, 7 miles south-east of Hebron. …

Fruits, “the Jezreelite,” was the owner of a portion of ground on the eastern slope of the hill of Jezreel ([2 Kings 9:25](#2Kgs.9.25), [26](#2Kgs.9.26)). This small “plat of ground” seems to have been all he possessed. It was a vineyard, and lay “hard by the palace of Ahab” ([1 Kings 21:1](#1Kgs.21.1), [2](#1Kgs.21.2)), who greatly coveted it. Naboth, however, refused on any terms to part with it to the king. He had inherited it from his fathers, and no Israelite could lawfully sell his property ([Lev. 25:23](#Lev.25.23)). Jezebel, Ahab’s wife, was grievously offended at Naboth’s refusal to part with his vineyard. By a crafty and cruel plot she compassed his death. …

The eldest of Aaron’s four sons ([Ex. 6:23](#Exod.6.23); [Num. 3:2](#Num.3.2)). He with his brothers and their father were consecrated as priests of Jehovah ([Ex. 28:1](#Exod.28.1)). He afterwards perished with Abihu for the sin of offering strange fire on the altar of burnt-offering ([Lev. 10:1](#Lev.10.1), [2](#Lev.10.2); [Num. 3:4](#Num.3.4); [26:60](#Num.26.60)).

The son and successor of Jeroboam, the king of Israel ([1 Kings 14:20](#1Kgs.14.20)). While engaged with all Israel in laying siege to Gibbethon, a town of southern Dan ([Josh. 19:44](#Josh.19.44)), a conspiracy broke out in his army, and he was slain by Baasha ([1 Kings 15:25-28](#1Kgs.15.25)), after a reign of two years (B.C. 955-953). The assassination of Nadab was followed by that of his whole house, and thus this great Ephraimite family became extinct ([1 Kings 15:29](#1Kgs.15.29)).
One of the sons of Shammai in the tribe of Judah ([1 Chr. 2:28](#1Chr.2.28), [30](#1Chr.2.30)).
Snorer, a Berothite, one of David’s heroes, and armour-bearer of Joab ([1 Chr. 11:39](#1Chr.11.39)).

King of the Ammonites in the time of Saul. The inhabitants of Jabesh-Gilead having been exposed to great danger from Nahash, sent messengers to Gibeah to inform Saul of their extremity. He promptly responded to the call, and gathering together an army he marched against Nahash. “And it came to pass that they which remained were scattered, so that two of them [the Ammonites] were not left together” ([1 Sam. 11:1-11](#1Sam.11.1)).

The father of Amasa, who was commander-in-chief of Abasolom’s army ([2 Sam. 17:25](#2Sam.17.25)). Jesse’s wife had apparently been first married to this man, to whom she bore Abigail and Zeruiah, who were thus David’s sisters, but only on the mother’s side ([1 Chr. 2:16](#1Chr.2.16)).
One of the four sons of Reuel, the son of Esau ([Gen. 36:13](#Gen.36.13), [17](#Gen.36.17)).
A Levite, one of the overseers of the sacred offerings of the temple ([2 Chr. 31:13](#2Chr.31.13)).
Hidden, one of the twelve spies sent out to explore the land of Canaan ([Num. 13:14](#Num.13.14)).

A son of Terah, and elder brother of Abraham ([Gen. 11:26](#Gen.11.26), [27](#Gen.11.27); [Josh. 24:2](#Josh.24.2), R.V.). He married Milcah, the daughter of his brother Haran, and remained in the land of his nativity on the east of the river Euphrates at Haran ([Gen. 11:27-32](#Gen.11.27)). A correspondence was maintained between the family of Abraham in Canaan and the relatives in the old ancestral home at Haran till the time of Jacob. When Jacob fled from Haran all intercourse between the two branches of the family came to an end ([Gen. 31:55](#Gen.31.55)). His grand-daughter Rebekah became Isaac’s wife (24:67).
The father of Terah, who was the father of Abraham ([Gen. 11:22-25](#Gen.11.22); [Luke 3:34](#Luke.3.34)).

Sorcerer, the son of Aminadab, and prince of the children of Judah at the time of the first numbering of the tribes in the wilderness ([Ex. 6:23](#Exod.6.23)). His sister Elisheba was the wife of Aaron. He died in the wilderness ([Num. 26:64](#Num.26.64), [65](#Num.26.65)). His name occurs in the Greek form Naasson in the genealogy of Christ (Matt, 1:4; [Luke 3:32](#Luke.3.32)).
Bitter; sad, a symbolical name which Naomi gave to herself because of her misfortunes ([Ruth 1:20](#Ruth.1.20)).

My wrestling, the fifth son of Jacob. His mother was Bilhah, Rachel’s handmaid ([Gen. 30:8](#Gen.30.8)). When Jacob went down into Egypt, Naphtali had four sons ([Gen. 46:24](#Gen.46.24)). Little is known of him as an individual.

A Hamitic tribe descended from Mizraim ([Gen. 10:13](#Gen.10.13)). Others identify this word with Napata, the name of the city and territory on the southern frontier of Mizraim, the modern Meroe, at the great bend of the Nile at Soudan. This city was the royal residence, it is said, of Queen Candace ([Acts 8:27](#Acts.8.27)). Here there are extensive and splendid ruins.
Daffodil, a Roman whom Paul salutes ([Rom. 16:11](#Rom.16.11)). He is supposed to have been the private secretary of the emperor Claudius. This is, however, quite uncertain.

A prophet in the reigns of David and Solomon ([2 Chr. 9:29](#2Chr.9.29)). He is first spoken of in connection with the arrangements David made for the building of the temple ([2 Sam. 7:2](#2Sam.7.2), [3](#2Sam.7.3), [17](#2Sam.7.17)), and next appears as the reprover of David on account of his sin with Bathsheba (12:1-14). He was charged with the education of Solomon (12:25), at whose inauguration to the throne he took a prominent part ([1 Kings 1:8](#1Kgs.1.8), [10](#1Kgs.1.10), [11](#1Kgs.1.11), [22](#1Kgs.1.22)-45). His two sons, Zabad ([1 Chr. 2:36](#1Chr.2.36)) and Azariah ([1 Kings 4:5](#1Kgs.4.5)) occupied places of honour at the king’s court. …
A son of David, by Bathsheba ([2 Sam. 5:14](#2Sam.5.14)), whose name appears in the genealogy of Mary, the mother of our Lord ([Luke 3:31](#Luke.3.31)).

A prophet in the reigns of David and Solomon ([2 Chr. 9:29](#2Chr.9.29)). He is first spoken of in connection with the arrangements David made for the building of the temple ([2 Sam. 7:2](#2Sam.7.2), [3](#2Sam.7.3), [17](#2Sam.7.17)), and next appears as the reprover of David on account of his sin with Bathsheba (12:1-14). He was charged with the education of Solomon (12:25), at whose inauguration to the throne he took a prominent part ([1 Kings 1:8](#1Kgs.1.8), [10](#1Kgs.1.10), [11](#1Kgs.1.11), [22](#1Kgs.1.22)-45). His two sons, Zabad ([1 Chr. 2:36](#1Chr.2.36)) and Azariah ([1 Kings 4:5](#1Kgs.4.5)) occupied places of honour at the king’s court. …

Given or gift of God, one of our Lord’s disciples, “of Cana in Galilee” ([John 21:2](#John.21.2)). He was “an Israelite indeed, in whom was no guile” (1:47, 48). His name occurs only in the Gospel of John, who in his list of the disciples never mentions Bartholomew, with whom he has consequently been identified. He was one of those to whom the Lord showed himself alive after his resurrection, at the Sea of Tiberias.
Ishmael’s eldest son ([Gen. 25:13](#Gen.25.13)), and the prince of an Israelitish tribe (16). He had a sister, Mahalath, who was one of Esau’s wives ([Gen. 28:9](#Gen.28.9); [36:3](#Gen.36.3)).
Sight; aspect, the father of Jeroboam, the king of Israel ([1 Kings 11:26](#1Kgs.11.26), etc.).

In the Babylonian orthography Nabu-kudur-uzur, which means “Nebo, protect the crown!” or the “frontiers.” In an inscription he styles himself “Nebo’s favourite.” He was the son and successor of Nabopolassar, who delivered Babylon from its dependence on Assyria and laid Nineveh in ruins. He was the greatest and most powerful of all the Babylonian kings. He married the daughter of Cyaxares, and thus the Median and Babylonian dynasties were united.

Adorer of Nebo, or Nebo saves me, the “Rabsaris,” or chief chamberlain, of the court of Babylon. He was one of those whom the king sent to release Jeremiah from prison in Jerusalem ([Jer. 39:13](#Jer.39.13)).

“the captain of the guard,” in rank next to the king, who appears prominent in directing affairs at the capture of Jerusalem ([2 Kings 25:8-20](#2Kgs.25.8); [Jer. 39:11](#Jer.39.11); [40:2-5](#Jer.40.2)). He showed kindness toward Jeremiah, as commanded by Nebuchadnezzar (40:1). Five years after this he again came to Jerusalem and carried captive seven hundred and forty-five more Jews.
Moved of Jehovah, one of the sons of Jeconiah ([1 Chr. 3:18](#1Chr.3.18)).

The son of Hachaliah ([Neh. 1:1](#Neh.1.1)), and probably of the tribe of Judah. His family must have belonged to Jerusalem ([Neh. 2:3](#Neh.2.3)). He was one of the “Jews of the dispersion,” and in his youth was appointed to the important office of royal cup-bearer at the palace of Shushan. The king, Artaxerxes Longimanus, seems to have been on terms of friendly familiarity with his attendant. Through his brother Hanani, and perhaps from other sources ([Neh. 1:2](#Neh.1.2); [2:3](#Neh.2.3)), he heard of the mournful and desolate condition of the Holy City, and was filled with sadness of heart. For many days he fasted and mourned and prayed for the place of his fathers’ sepulchres. …
Copper, the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem, and the wife of Jehoiakin ([2 Kings 24:8](#2Kgs.24.8)), king of Judah.
A Reubenite, a son of Eliab, and brother of Dathan and Abiram ([Num. 26:9](#Num.26.9)).

Light, the father of Kish ([1 Chr. 8:33](#1Chr.8.33)). [1 Sam. 14:51](#1Sam.14.51) should be read, “Kish, the father of Saul, and Ner, the father of Abner, were the sons of Abiel.” And hence this Kish and Ner were brothers, and Saul and Abner were first cousins (comp. [1 Chr. 9:36](#1Chr.9.36)).

Another of the “princes,” who bore the title of “Rabmag.” He was one of those who were sent to release Jeremiah from prison ([Jer. 39:13](#Jer.39.13)) by “the captain of the guard.” He was a Babylonian grandee of high rank. From profane history and the inscriptions, we are led to conclude that he was the Neriglissar who murdered Evil-merodach, the son of Nebuchadnezzar, and succeeded him on the throne of Babylon (B.C. 559-556). He was married to a daughter of Nebuchadnezzar. The ruins of a palace, the only one on the right bank of the Euphrates, bear inscriptions denoting that it was built by this king. …
The son of Zuar, chief of the tribe of Issachar at the Exodus ([Num. 1:8](#Num.1.8); [2:5](#Num.2.5)).
A priest who blew the trumpet before the ark when it was brought up to Jerusalem ([1 Chr. 15:24](#1Chr.15.24)).
A temple porter, of the family of the Korhites ([1 Chr. 26:4](#1Chr.26.4)).
One of the “princes” appointed by Jehoshaphat to teach the law through the cities of Judah ([2 Chr. 17:7](#2Chr.17.7)).
A chief Levite in the time of Josiah ([2 Chr. 35:9](#2Chr.35.9)).
A priest’s son who bore a trumpet at the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem ([Neh. 12:36](#Neh.12.36)).
A Levite sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the law ([2 Chr. 17:8](#2Chr.17.8)).
Conqueror, one of the seven deacons appointed in the apostolic Church ([Acts 6:1-6](#Acts.6.1)). Nothing further is known of him.

The people is victor, a Pharisee and a member of the Sanhedrin. He is first noticed as visiting Jesus by night ([John 3:1-21](#John.3.1)) for the purpose of learning more of his doctrines, which our Lord then unfolded to him, giving prominence to the necessity of being “born again.” He is next met with in the Sanhedrin (7:50-52), where he protested against the course they were taking in plotting against Christ. Once more he is mentioned as taking part in the preparation for the anointing and burial of the body of Christ ([John 19:39](#John.19.39)). We hear nothing more of him. There can be little doubt that he became a true disciple.
The victory of the people, a proselyte of Antioch, one of the seven deacons ([Acts 6:5](#Acts.6.5)).

Firm, a descendant of Cush, the son of Ham. He was the first who claimed to be a “mighty one in the earth.” Babel was the beginning of his kingdom, which he gradually enlarged ([Gen. 10:8-10](#Gen.10.8)). The “land of Nimrod” ([Micah 5:6](#Mic.5.6)) is a designation of Assyria or of Shinar, which is a part of it.
Saved. Jehu was “the son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi” ([2 Kings 9:2](#2Kgs.9.2); comp. [1 Kings 19:16](#1Kgs.19.16)).
A Levite who returned from Babylon ([Ezra 8:33](#Ezra.8.33)).

A false prophetess who assisted Tobiah and Sanballat against the Jews ([Neh. 6:14](#Neh.6.14)). Being bribed by them, she tried to stir up discontent among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and so to embarrass Nehemiah in his great work of rebuilding the ruined walls of the city.

Rest, (Heb. Noah) the grandson of Methuselah ([Gen. 5:25-29](#Gen.5.25)), who was for two hundred and fifty years contemporary with Adam, and the son of Lamech, who was about fifty years old at the time of Adam’s death. This patriarch is rightly regarded as the connecting link between the old and the new world. He is the second great progenitor of the human family.

Rest, (Heb. Noah) the grandson of Methuselah ([Gen. 5:25-29](#Gen.5.25)), who was for two hundred and fifty years contemporary with Adam, and the son of Lamech, who was about fifty years old at the time of Adam’s death. This patriarch is rightly regarded as the connecting link between the old and the new world. He is the second great progenitor of the human family.
Splendour, one of David’s sons, born at Jerusalem ([1 Chr. 3:7](#1Chr.3.7)).
Beyond the fact that he was the father of Joshua nothing more is known of him ([Ex. 33:11](#Exod.33.11)).

An Israelite who was chief in the household of King Ahab ([1 Kings 18:3](#1Kgs.18.3)). Amid great spiritual degeneracy he maintained his fidelity to God, and interposed to protect The Lord’s prophets, an hundred of whom he hid at great personal risk in a cave (4, 13). Ahab seems to have held Obadiah in great honour, although he had no sympathy with his piety (5, 6, 7). The last notice of him is his bringing back tidings to Ahab that Elijah, whom he had so long sought for, was at hand (9-16). “Go,” said Elijah to him, when he met him in the way, “go tell thy lord, Behold, Elijah is here.”
A Levite, after the Captivity ([1 Chr. 9:16](#1Chr.9.16)).
A chief of the tribe of Issachar ([1 Chr. 7:3](#1Chr.7.3)).
A Gadite who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:9](#1Chr.12.9)).
A prince of Zebulun in the time of David ([1 Chr. 27:19](#1Chr.27.19)).
One of the princes sent by Jehoshaphat to instruct the people in the law ([2 Chr. 17:7](#2Chr.17.7)).
A Levite who superintended the repairs of the temple under Josiah ([2 Chr. 34:12](#2Chr.34.12)).
One who accompanied Ezra on the return from Babylon ([Ezra 8:9](#Ezra.8.9)).
A son of Boaz and Ruth ([Ruth 4:21](#Ruth.4.21), [22](#Ruth.4.22)), and the grandfather of David ([Matt. 1:5](#Matt.1.5)).
A keeper of camels, an Ishmaelite who was “over the camels” in the time of David ([1 Chr. 27:30](#1Chr.27.30)).
A prophet in the time of Ahaz and Pekah ([2 Chr. 28:9-15](#2Chr.28.9)).

Gigantic, the king of Bashan, who was defeated by Moses in a pitched battle at Edrei, and was slain along with his sons ([Deut. 1:4](#Deut.1.4)), and whose kingdom was given to the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh ([Num. 21:32-35](#Num.21.32); [Deut. 3:1-13](#Deut.3.1)). His bedstead (or rather sarcophagus) was of iron (or ironstone), 9 cubits in length and 4 cubits in breadth. His overthrow was afterwards celebrated in song ([Ps. 135:11](#Ps.135.11); [136:20](#Ps.136.20)).
United, or power, the third son of Simeon ([Gen. 46:10](#Gen.46.10)).
A house; tent, the fourth son of Zerubbabel ([1 Chr. 3:20](#1Chr.3.20)).
A Roman Christian whom Paul salutes ([Rom. 16:15](#Rom.16.15)).
Eloquent, the son of Eliphaz, who was Esau’s eldest son ([Gen. 36:11-15](#Gen.36.11)).

Servant of Jehovah. When Elah was murdered by Zimri at Tirzah ([1 Kings 16:15-27](#1Kgs.16.15)), Omri, his captain, was made king (B.C. 931). For four years there was continued opposition to his reign, Tibni, another claimant to the throne, leading the opposing party; but at the close of that period all his rivals were defeated, and he became king of Israel, “Tibni died and Omri reigned” (B.C. 927). By his vigour and power he gained great eminence and consolidated the kingdom. He fixed his dynasty on the throne so firmly that it continued during four succeeding reigns. Tirza was for six years the seat of his government. …
Strong, the second son of Judah ([Gen. 38:4-10](#Gen.38.4); comp. [Deut. 25:5](#Deut.25.5); [Matt. 22:24](#Matt.22.24)). He died before the going down of Jacob and his family into Egypt.

Useful, a slave who, after robbing his master Philemon (q.v.) at Colosse, fled to Rome, where he was converted by the apostle Paul, who sent him back to his master with the epistle which bears his name. In it he beseeches Philemon to receive his slave as a “faithful and beloved brother.” Paul offers to pay to Philemon anything his slave had taken, and to bear the wrong he had done him. He was accompanied on his return by Tychicus, the bearer of the Epistle to the Colossians ([Philemon 1](#Phlm.1.1):16, 18).

Bringing profit, an Ephesian Christian who showed great kindness to Paul at Rome. He served him in many things, and had oft refreshed him. Paul expresses a warm interest in him and his household ([2 Tim. 1:16-18](#2Tim.1.16); [4:19](#2Tim.4.19)).
One of the sons of Joktan ([Gen. 10:29](#Gen.10.29)).

Raven, a prince of Midian, who, being defeated by Gideon and put to straits, was slain along with Zeeb ([Judg. 7:20-25](#Judg.7.20)). Many of the Midianites perished along with him ([Ps. 83:9](#Ps.83.9); [Isa. 10:26](#Isa.10.26)).
Ash or pine, the son of Jerahmeel ([1 Chr. 2:25](#1Chr.2.25)).

Agile; also called Ornan [1 Chr. 21:15](#1Chr.21.15), a Jebusite who dwelt in Jerusalem before it was taken by the Israelites. The destroying angel, sent to punish David for his vanity in taking a census of the people, was stayed in his work of destruction near a threshing-floor belonging to Araunah which was situated on Mount Moriah. Araunah offered it to David as a free gift, together with the oxen and the threshing instruments; but the king insisted on purchasing it at its full price ([2 Sam. 24:24](#2Sam.24.24); [1 Chr. 21:24](#1Chr.21.24), [25](#1Chr.21.25)), for, according to the law of sacrifices, he could not offer to God what cost him nothing. On the same place Solomon afterwards erected the temple ([2 Sam. 24:16](#2Sam.24.16); [2 Chr. 3:1](#2Chr.3.1)).

Forelock or fawn, a Moabitess, the wife of Chilion ([Ruth 1:4](#Ruth.1.4); [4:10](#Ruth.4.10)). On the death of her husband she accompanied Naomi, her mother-in-law, part of the way to Bethlehem, and then returned to Moab.
A lion of Jehovah, a son of Shemaiah, and one of the temple porters in the time of David ([1 Chr. 26:7](#1Chr.26.7)). He was a “mighty man of valour.”

Lion of God, the first of the judges. His wife Achsah was the daughter of Caleb ([Josh. 15:16](#Josh.15.16), [17](#Josh.15.17); [Judg. 1:13](#Judg.1.13)). He gained her hand as a reward for his bravery in leading a successful expedition against Debir (q.v.). Some thirty years after the death of Joshua, the Israelites fell under the subjection of Chushan-rishathaim (q.v.), the king of Mesopotamia. He oppressed them for full eight years, when they “cried” unto Jehovah, and Othniel was raised up to be their deliverer. He was the younger brother of Caleb ([Judg. 3:8](#Judg.3.8), [9](#Judg.3.9)-11). He is the only judge mentioned connected with the tribe of Judah. Under him the land had rest forty years.
One of David’s brothers; the sixth son of Jesse ([1 Chr. 2:15](#1Chr.2.15)).
Hearing, one of the sons of Gad; also called Ezbon ([Gen. 46:16](#Gen.46.16); [Num. 26:16](#Num.26.16)).
Opening of the Lord, “the Arbite,” one of David’s heroes ([2 Sam. 23:35](#2Sam.23.35)); called also Naarai, [1 Chr. 11:37](#1Chr.11.37).
God allots, a prince of the tribe of Asher ([Num. 1:13](#Num.1.13)), in the wilderness.
Governor of Moab, a person whose descendants returned from the Captivity and assisted in rebuilding Jerusalem ([Ezra 2:6](#Ezra.2.6); [8:4](#Ezra.8.4); [10:30](#Ezra.10.30)).

Separated, the second son of Reuben ([1 Chr. 5:3](#1Chr.5.3)); called Phallu, [Gen. 46:9](#Gen.46.9). He was the father of the Phalluites ([Ex. 6:14](#Exod.6.14); [Num. 26:5](#Num.26.5), [8](#Num.26.8)).
Deliverance from the Lord, one of the spies representing the tribe of Benjamin ([Num. 13:9](#Num.13.9)).
Deliverance of God, the prince of Issachar who assisted “to divide the land by inheritance” ([Num. 34:26](#Num.34.26)).
Strong-fisted, a son of Haman, slain in Shushan ([Esther 9:9](#Esth.9.9)).
An interpreter of the law, the eldest of Haman’s sons, slain in Shushan ([Esther 9:7](#Esth.9.7)).
Flourishing, the father of Jehoshaphat, appointed to provide monthly supplies for Solomon from the tribe of Issachar ([1 Kings 4:17](#1Kgs.4.17)).
Clearing, one of the sons of Japhlet, of the tribe of Asher ([1 Chr. 7:33](#1Chr.7.33)).
A Christian at Rome to whom Paul sent salutations ([Rom. 16:14](#Rom.16.14)).

'=Saul (q.v.) was born about the same time as our Lord. His circumcision-name was Saul, and probably the name Paul was also given to him in infancy “for use in the Gentile world,” as “Saul” would be his Hebrew home-name. He was a native of Tarsus, the capital of Cilicia, a Roman province in the south-east of Asia Minor. That city stood on the banks of the river Cydnus, which was navigable thus far; hence it became a centre of extensive commercial traffic with many countries along the shores of the Mediterranean, as well as with the countries of central Asia Minor. It thus became a city distinguished for the wealth of its inhabitants.
Redeemed of God, the son of Ammihud, a prince of Naphtali ([Num. 34:28](#Num.34.28)).
Rock of redemption, the father of Gamaliel and prince of Manasseh at the time of the Exodus ([Num. 1:10](#Num.1.10); [2:20](#Num.2.20)).
The father of Zebudah, who was the wife of Josiah and mother of king Jehoiakim ([2 Kings 23:36](#2Kgs.23.36)).
. The father of Joel, ruler of the half-tribe of Manasseh ([1 Chr. 27:20](#1Chr.27.20)).

Open-eyed, the son of Remaliah a captain in the army of Pekahiah, king of Israel, whom he slew, with the aid of a band of Gileadites, and succeeded (B.C. 758) on the throne ([2 Kings 15:25](#2Kgs.15.25)). Seventeen years after this he entered into an alliance with Rezin, king of Syria, and took part with him in besieging Jerusalem ([2 Kings 15:37](#2Kgs.15.37); [16:5](#2Kgs.16.5)). But Tiglath-pilser, who was in alliance with Ahaz, king of Judah, came up against Pekah, and carried away captive many of the inhabitants of his kingdom ([2 Kings 15:29](#2Kgs.15.29)). This was the beginning of the “Captivity.” Soon after this Pekah was put to death by Hoshea, the son of Elah, who usurped the throne ([2 Kings 15:30](#2Kgs.15.30); [16:1-9](#2Kgs.16.1). Comp. [Isa. 7:16](#Isa.7.16); [8:4](#Isa.8.4); [9:12](#Isa.9.12)). He is supposed by some to have been the “shephard” mentioned in [Zech. 11:16](#Zech.11.16).

The Lord opened his eyes, the son and successor of Menahem on the throne of Israel. He was murdered in the royal palace of Samaria by Pekah, one of the captains of his army ([2 Kings 15:23-26](#2Kgs.15.23)), after a reign of two years (B.C. 761-759). He “did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord.”
A Levite who expounded the law ([Neh. 8:7](#Neh.8.7)).
One of the twenty-five princes of the people against whom Ezekiel prophesied on account of their wicked counsel ([Ezek. 11:1-13](#Ezek.11.1)).
A son of Hananiah and grandson of Zerubbabel ([1 Chr. 3:21](#1Chr.3.21)).

Division, one of the sons of Eber; so called because “in his days was the earth divided” ([Gen. 10:25](#Gen.10.25)). Possibly he may have lived at the time of the dispersion from Babel. But more probably the reference is to the dispersion of the two races which sprang from Eber, the one spreading towards Mesopotamia and Syria, and the other southward into Arabia.
A Benjamite who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:3](#1Chr.12.3)).
A Reubenite whose son was one of the conspirators against Moses and Aaron ([Num. 16:1](#Num.16.1)).
One of the sons of Jonathan ([1 Chr. 2:33](#1Chr.2.33)).
One whose descendants returned with Zerubbabel ([Ezra 2:55](#Ezra.2.55)); called also Perida ([Neh. 7:57](#Neh.7.57)).
A female Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes ([Rom. 16:12](#Rom.16.12)). She is spoken of as “beloved,” and as having “laboured much in the Lord.”
The chief of one of the priestly courses (the nineteenth) in the time of David ([1 Chr. 24:16](#1Chr.24.16)).
